253.title: Al-Wakil, the Trustee
253.hook: the Trustee, the one you hand things over to, after doing your part (Tirmidhi)
253.howItsDone: Muslims describe tawakkul as taking every reasonable step and then relying on God for the outcome, and many say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil in hard moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative. Your line was nothing small is lost. Did you thank someone out loud for something tiny? Day two hundred fifty-three.

A man comes to see the Prophet. He gets off his camel, and stops. He's got a question, and it's a real one. Should he tie the camel up, and then trust God to keep it? Or should he leave it loose, and trust God, full stop? If he ties it, is he trusting less? If he doesn't, is he being a fool? You've had your own version of this. You studied, or you didn't. You locked the door, or you didn't. How much is on you, and how much do you hand over? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave him an answer in four words that people still quote more than fourteen centuries later. Today: tawakkul.
screen: `A MAN AND HIS CAMEL.` → `TIE IT, OR TRUST?` → `FOUR WORDS.`

segments.voice: The answer, in the collection of at-Tirmidhi: tie it, and trust. Both. In that order. Tawakkul is the word for that trust, and it comes from the same root as today's name, al-Wakil, the Trustee. In ordinary Arabic, a wakil is the person you hand your affairs to: an agent, a representative, the one who handles it when you can't. Calling God al-Wakil means he is the One you hand things over to. But the hadith sets the order. First you do your part. Tie the rope. Study for the test. See the doctor. Then you let go of the outcome, because it was never fully in your hands. That's tawakkul. Not doing nothing. Doing what's yours, and then letting the rest rest. The Qur'an promises, in Pickthall's words: "And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him." Another hadith in Tirmidhi adds a picture. If you trusted God as you truly should, he would provide for you as he provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and come back full at evening. Notice, the birds go out. They don't sit in the nest waiting. And there's a phrase many Muslims say when things are heavy: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil. God is enough for us, and he is the best Trustee. The Qur'an gives it to believers who were told an army was gathering against them. It's said after the work is done, when there's nothing left to do but hand it over.
screen: `TIE IT, AND TRUST.` · `A WAKIL HANDLES YOUR AFFAIRS.` · `THE BIRDS GO OUT.` · `GOD IS ENOUGH FOR US.` · then, large: `TIE THE CAMEL, THEN TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your part, then hand it over. Sit, and think of one thing you're worried about. Ask yourself honestly: what's the rope I can tie? One email, one call, one appointment, one conversation. Name it, and decide when you'll do it. Then look at what's left, the part that isn't yours to control. Picture setting it down. If you pray, you can say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil. If not, just breathe out, and let it rest. The bell holds the time.
Tawakkul. Trust in God, from the same root as al-Wakil, the Trustee: do your part, then hand over the rest. Today's word.
Your line: tie the camel, then trust. Today, tie your one rope, and then, when the worry comes back, remind it that the rest is handed over. Day two hundred fifty-three.

254.title: Al-Hayy, al-Qayyum
254.hook: the Living, the Self-Sustaining, on whom everything rests (2:255)
254.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi before sleep, after each obligatory prayer and when leaving the house, and call on God as ya Hayyu ya Qayyum in times of need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawakkul, trust, and al-Wakil, the Trustee. Your line was tie the camel, then trust. Did you tie your one rope, and let the rest go? Day two hundred fifty-four.

Right now, something is holding you up. The chair. The floor under the chair. The building under the floor, the ground under the building, the planet turning under all of it, and you're not thinking about any of it. You only notice what holds you when it wobbles. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once asked a companion, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, which verse of the Qur'an is the greatest. Ubayy answered with a verse that begins with two names, the Living and the one who holds everything up. And the Prophet, the hadith in Sahih Muslim says, struck him on the chest, pleased, and congratulated him on his knowledge. Today, those two names, and the first of them for our word: Al-Hayy.
screen: `WHAT'S HOLDING YOU UP?` → `THE GREATEST VERSE.` → `TWO NAMES.`

segments.voice: The verse is Ayat al-Kursi, the Verse of the Throne, 2:255. In Pickthall's translation it begins: "Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him." The Alive is al-Hayy, from hayat, life. Everything else that lives borrowed its life and will give it back. Al-Hayy's life isn't borrowed. It doesn't start and it doesn't end. The Eternal is al-Qayyum, and here Pickthall picks one side of a rich word. It comes from q-w-m, to stand. Al-Qayyum is the One who stands by himself, needing nothing, and who keeps everything else standing. The Self-Subsisting, the Sustainer. Then comes the line that makes the names concrete: neither slumber nor sleep overtakes him. Think about what that means. Every guard falls asleep. Every parent eventually dozes off in the chair by the crib. The one holding up the heavens and the earth never does. The verse goes on: his throne, his kursi, spans the heavens and the earth, and guarding them doesn't tire him. That's why so many Muslims recite this one verse before sleeping. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says whoever recites it at bedtime has a guardian from God through the night. You sleep, because he doesn't. And there's a du'a from the Prophet, in at-Tirmidhi, that calls on these two names together: ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum, O Living, O Sustainer, by your mercy I seek help. Some scholars even suggested these two together are the greatest name of all.
screen: `AYAT AL-KURSI — 2:255.` · `AL-HAYY — LIFE NOT BORROWED.` · `AL-QAYYUM — KEEPS ALL STANDING.` · `NO SLUMBER, NO SLEEP.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING RESTS ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit and feel what holds you up. Let your weight drop into the chair or the floor. Feel where you're touching it: your feet, your legs, your back. Let the floor take a little more of you than it usually does. Then go one layer out: the ground under the floor. Then the whole earth under that. Notice that you didn't have to hold any of it up. If you pray, you can say, quietly, ya Hayyu, ya Qayyum. The bell holds the time.
Al-Hayy. The Living, whose life is not borrowed, named together with al-Qayyum, the One who keeps everything standing. Today's word.
Your line: everything rests on him. Tonight, as you lie down, feel the bed hold you, and notice you're allowed to sleep. Day two hundred fifty-four.

255.title: An-Nur, the Light
255.hook: the Light of the heavens and the earth, light upon light (24:35)
255.howItsDone: The Light Verse is one of the most often calligraphed verses in mosques and homes, and many Muslims say the Prophet's du'a for light, often on the way to the dawn prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Hayy and al-Qayyum, the Living and the one who keeps all standing. Your line was everything rests on him. Did you feel the bed hold you last night? Day two hundred fifty-five.

Picture a house in Medina, fourteen hundred years ago, after dark. No electricity, no streetlights. In the wall there's a small hollow, a niche, and in it a clay lamp with a wick floating in olive oil. It's the only light in the room. Everyone's face turns toward it. You can see the edge of the flame, the glow on the wall, the little circle of the world it makes safe. Now imagine someone takes that ordinary, everyday lamp, the one every listener had in their own home, and uses it to describe God. That's what one of the most famous verses in the Qur'an does. Today: An-Nur.
screen: `A HOUSE AFTER DARK.` → `A LAMP IN A NICHE.` → `A PICTURE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Surah 24 is called an-Nur, the Light, and its thirty-fifth verse is called the Light Verse. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Then the picture. His light is like a niche, and in the niche a lamp. The lamp is in a glass, and the glass is like a shining star. The lamp is lit from the oil of a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, oil so pure it would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. And then two words: "Light upon light." In Arabic, nurun 'ala nur. Look at the layers: a niche that gathers the light, a glass that makes it shine like a star, oil that nearly lights itself, a flame. Each one adds to the one before. Light upon light. The verse ends by saying God guides to his light whom he wills, and that he strikes these likenesses for people. Commentators have read the picture in many ways. Some say the lamp is the light of guidance in a believer's heart: the chest is the niche, the heart the glass, faith the flame. Some say it's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, or the Qur'an. The great scholar al-Ghazali wrote a whole book on this one verse, the Niche of Lights. And the Prophet had a du'a asking God to put light in his heart, in his hearing, in his sight, on his right and his left, above and below him, and to make him light. He didn't ask for a lamp. He asked to be one.
screen: `THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND EARTH.` · `NICHE, GLASS, OIL, FLAME.` · `THE HEART, THE PROPHET, THE BOOK.` · `MAKE ME LIGHT.` · then, large: `LIGHT UPON LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit near a lamp or a window. Move there now if you can. Let your eyes rest on the light, softly, not staring. Notice the layers: the source, the glass or the shade, the glow it throws on the wall, the light landing on your hands. Light upon light. Then close your eyes and notice that the light is still there, faintly, through your eyelids. If you pray, you can ask God, an-Nur, for light in your heart. The bell holds the time.
An-Nur. The Light: the Light of the heavens and the earth, pictured as a lamp in a niche, light upon light. Today's word.
Your line: light upon light. Today, every time you switch on a light, let it remind you of the lamp in the niche, just for a second. Day two hundred fifty-five.

256.title: As-Sabur, the Patient
256.hook: the Patient, the last of the traditional list, who waits for us
256.howItsDone: The names are often recited as a whole list, sometimes sung, and many Muslims memorize the ninety-nine, ending with as-Sabur; patience, sabr, is praised throughout the Qur'an as a quality believers work to build.

segments.voice: Yesterday, An-Nur, the Light, the lamp in the niche. Your line was light upon light. Did a light switch remind you, even once? Day two hundred fifty-six.

Think about the most patient person you've ever known. Maybe a teacher who explained the same thing to you five times without a sigh. A grandparent who let you help in the kitchen when you were four and useless. A friend who waited years for you to come around, and never once said, finally. Patience like that is rare, and you remember it for life. For twenty-five days we've been walking through the most beautiful names of God. The best-known list of ninety-nine, the one in the collection of at-Tirmidhi, ends with a name that's easy to miss at the bottom of the page. It's the last word of the list, and it's a good one to end on. Today: As-Sabur.
screen: `THE MOST PATIENT PERSON YOU KNOW.` → `TWENTY-FIVE DAYS OF NAMES.` → `THE LAST ONE ON THE LIST.`

segments.voice: As-Sabur comes from sabr, the word for patience and steadfastness. Its root means to hold back, to bind, to keep yourself steady. For people, sabr is hard work: holding on through grief, holding back from the easy wrong, holding steady when nothing changes. The Qur'an says it often, and in Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." But what does it mean for God to be sabur? Scholars say it's this: he sees what people do, has every power to answer at once, and doesn't hurry. He gives time. It's close to al-Halim, the Forbearing, from a few days ago, and scholars draw a fine line between them, but both say the same warm thing. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put it in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari: no one is more patient with hurtful words than God. People say the worst things about him, and still he gives them health, and still he feeds them. So many Muslims hear As-Sabur as the God who waits. Who waits for the person who keeps promising to come back to prayer, and for the one who wandered off years ago. Who keeps giving health and food, the hadith says, even to people who speak against Him. Now look back at the whole part. Twenty-five days: Allah, the name itself, then ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, the King, the Holy, Peace, the Maker, the Forgiving, the Provider, the Opener, the Knower, the Hearing and Seeing, the Gentle, the Forbearing, the Loving, the Appreciative, the Trustee, the Living, the Light. And at the end of the list, the Patient, still waiting.
screen: `SABR — TO HOLD STEADY.` · `ALLAH IS WITH THE STEADFAST.` · `NO ONE MORE PATIENT THAN GOD.` · `TWENTY-FIVE DAYS OF NAMES.` · then, large: `HE WAITS FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with yourself. Sit, and let one thing come to mind that you're frustrated with yourself about. The habit you keep breaking. The thing you still haven't done. Notice the voice that says, what's wrong with you. Now try talking to yourself the way that most patient person talked to you. Slower. Kinder. Not letting you off, just not in a hurry. If you pray, you can call on God as ya Sabur. The bell holds the time.
As-Sabur. The Patient: the One who sees, holds all power, and still waits. The last name on the traditional list. Today's word.

Your line: he waits for you. Tomorrow we leave the names and go back to the story, to Medina, where the Prophet has just arrived. Today, give yourself one extra minute you'd usually deny yourself. Day two hundred fifty-six.

257.title: Quba, the first mosque
257.hook: on arrival he helps build the first mosque with his own hands (9:108)
257.howItsDone: Pilgrims to Medina visit the Quba mosque, many making wudu at home first and praying two units there, as the Prophet did on Saturdays; the mosque has been rebuilt and enlarged many times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, As-Sabur, the Patient, the last name on the list. Your line was he waits for you. Did you give yourself that extra minute? Day two hundred fifty-seven, and back to the story.

We left the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on the road. After thirteen years of mockery and pressure in Mecca, he's slipped out of the city by night with Abu Bakr, hidden in a cave, and crossed the desert. The people of Medina have been walking out every morning to the edge of the lava fields to watch for him, going home when the heat gets too much. Then one day a lookout sees white figures shimmering on the road, and shouts. He's here. But before he enters the city itself, he stops at a village of palm groves on its southern edge, and stays there for some days. And the first thing he does is build. Today: Quba.
screen: `OUT OF MECCA BY NIGHT.` → `MEDINA WATCHING THE ROAD.` → `A VILLAGE ON THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Quba was a village of date farms a few miles from the heart of Medina. The Prophet stayed there with a local family, and in those days the first mosque of the new community went up. Muslims count it as the first mosque built in Islam. It wasn't grand. A plot of ground marked out, low walls, a place to face the direction of prayer together. And the early accounts say the Prophet carried stones for it himself, with his companions, not standing to one side while others worked. The Qur'an speaks of a mosque founded on reverence for God from its very first day, and says it is more fitting to stand in to pray, with people in it who love to purify themselves. Commentators differ over which mosque the verse means. Many say Quba. A hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet pointing to his own mosque in Medina. Some scholars say it praises both. Either way, what it praises is the foundation, not the building: reverence, from the first day. And Quba stayed close to him. Sahih al-Bukhari says he used to go to Quba every Saturday, walking or riding, and pray two units of prayer there. Another hadith, in at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, says a prayer in the mosque of Quba carries the reward of an 'umrah, the lesser pilgrimage. That little farm-village mosque was where the new life began: not with a speech, but with a man lifting stones next to everyone else.
screen: `A VILLAGE OF DATE FARMS.` · `HE CARRIED STONES HIMSELF.` · `FOUNDED ON REVERENCE.` · `EVERY SATURDAY TO QUBA.` · then, large: `LIFT A STONE TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help build or tidy something shared, starting now in your head. Sit, and think of a space you share with other people. A kitchen, an office, a stairwell, a park, a prayer room, a group chat that's gotten messy. Picture one small thing in it that nobody's handling. Picture yourself doing it, with your own hands, without waiting to be asked. Then just sit with the thought that the first mosque was built this way. The bell holds the time.
Quba. The village at the edge of Medina where the Prophet stopped first, and where the first mosque went up. Today's word.
Your line: lift a stone too. Today, do the one shared chore you pictured, and do it next to someone if you can. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

258.title: The mosque of palm trunks
258.hook: in Medina the Prophet's Mosque is built of mud brick and palm, and he carries bricks
258.howItsDone: The Prophet's Mosque in Medina is the second holiest mosque for Muslims, and many pilgrims visit it; many local mosques around the world are still simple rooms, often with carpets on the floor and no furniture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quba, the first mosque, stones carried by the Prophet himself. Your line was lift a stone too. Did you do the shared chore? Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Today in Medina, the Prophet's Mosque is enormous. White marble, a sea of columns, air conditioning, room for many hundreds of thousands of people, green dome over his grave. Pilgrims come from every country on earth. But stand in it and try to picture the first version. A patch of ground where dates were laid out to dry. A wall of sun-dried mud brick about head height. Tree trunks for pillars. Palm branches for a roof, which leaked when it rained. A floor of earth and pebbles. And among the people carrying the bricks from the kiln, sweating in the heat, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself. Today: the mosque of palm trunks.
screen: `MARBLE AND A GREEN DOME.` → `MUD, PALM, PEBBLES.` → `HE CARRIED BRICKS.`

segments.voice: The story is in Sahih al-Bukhari. When the Prophet reached the center of Medina, the land where his camel knelt belonged to two orphan boys. They offered it to him as a gift. He insisted on paying for it. The plot had some palm trees and some old graves. The trees were cut down, and their trunks lined up to make the pillars. The walls went up in mud brick. The roof was palm leaves laid over beams. And the companions carried the bricks, chanting a short rhyming verse as they worked, and the Prophet carried bricks with them and chanted along. It was built plainly, and on purpose. It had to be. There was no money. But even later, when there was, the mosque stayed simple for a long time. A floor of pebbles, so that when it rained, people prayed in mud. A hadith even describes the Prophet rising from prostration at the dawn prayer one Ramadan with mud and water on his forehead. And one palm trunk has its own story. Before there was a pulpit, the Prophet used to lean against a trunk when he gave the Friday sermon. When a small wooden pulpit was built and he stepped up onto it, Sahih al-Bukhari says the trunk cried out, like a child, and the Prophet came down and put his hand on it until it quieted. The house of God, in Medina, began as the plainest building in town. Everything that came later was built on that.
screen: `TWO ORPHANS' LAND, PAID FOR.` · `TRUNKS FOR PILLARS, PALM FOR A ROOF.` · `A FLOOR OF PEBBLES AND MUD.` · `THE TRUNK THAT CRIED.` · then, large: `BUILT PLAINLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit on the floor for this session. If you can, get down there now. No cushion needed, or just a thin one. Feel how close you are to the ground. This is how the first Muslims prayed in that mosque, on earth and pebbles, shoulder to shoulder. Notice what it's like to have nothing between you and the floor but your own clothes. Let it be plain. The bell holds the time.
The mosque of palm trunks. The first Prophet's Mosque in Medina: mud brick, palm pillars, a palm-leaf roof, and a floor of pebbles. Today's word.

259.title: Brothers across tribes
259.hook: each Meccan migrant is paired as a brother with a Medinan helper, who shares his home
259.howItsDone: Muslims remember the Ansar and Muhajirun as models of hospitality and brotherhood, and many communities today pair newcomers, converts or refugees with established families in the same spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mosque of palm trunks, mud brick and a pebble floor. Your line was built plainly. What did you choose the plain version of? Day two hundred fifty-nine, the end of a week.

Imagine arriving in a new city with nothing. You left your house, your business, your savings, sometimes your family, because staying had become impossible. You don't know the streets. You don't know the farming, because back home everyone traded. That was the situation of the Muslims who followed the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ from Mecca. And now imagine the other side. You live in Medina. You have a house, a date grove, a family. And one day someone knocks, and you're told: this man is your brother now. Not as a figure of speech. Your brother. What happened next is one of the most remembered stories in the whole seerah. Today: the Ansar.
screen: `ARRIVING WITH NOTHING.` → `A KNOCK AT THE DOOR.` → `THIS MAN IS YOUR BROTHER.`

segments.voice: The people who left Mecca are called the Muhajirun, the emigrants. The people of Medina who took them in are called the Ansar, the helpers. The word comes from nasr, help, support, and it became a title of honor they carried for the rest of their lives. The Prophet paired them up, one emigrant with one helper, as brothers. For a time, early on, these brothers even inherited from each other, until later verses returned inheritance to family. Sahih al-Bukhari tells one pairing in detail. Abd ar-Rahman ibn 'Awf, from Mecca, was made brother to Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi', from Medina. Sa'd said to him: I'm the richest of the Ansar. I'll split my wealth with you, half and half. And Abd ar-Rahman answered: may God bless you in your family and your wealth. Just show me where the market is. He went, traded, and before long was on his feet. One brother gave everything. The other took only what he needed. The Qur'an praises the Ansar in a verse many Muslims know: they love those who came to them, they feel no envy for what the newcomers are given, and they prefer others over themselves even when they themselves are poor. And remember who the Ansar were. Two tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, who had fought each other for years. Now they were brothers to each other, and to strangers. Look back over this week: tie the camel, then trust; the Living who holds everything up; light upon light; the Patient who waits. Then the story again: lift a stone, build plainly, and now, open the house.
screen: `MUHAJIRUN AND ANSAR.` · `HALF OF ALL I HAVE.` · `JUST SHOW ME THE MARKET.` · `THEY PREFER OTHERS.` · then, large: `BROTHERS BY CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share something with someone new. Sit, and think of someone in your world who's recently arrived. A new coworker. A neighbor who just moved in. A kid who's new at school. Someone new to your mosque, or your gym, or your city. Picture them, and what they might be missing: a name, a recommendation, a meal, a map. Pick one thing you could share with them this week. Then sit with what it's like to be on either side of that knock at the door. The bell holds the time.
